title: Kosmos 954 vs Chernobyl
hook: A 50kg nuclear reactor fell from orbit onto Canada, scattering fragments hot enough to kill you in hours. In 1978, eight years before Chernobyl.

substance.claim: Kosmos 954 was powered by a BES-5 nuclear reactor containing approximately 50 kg of highly-enriched uranium with over 90% uranium-235.
substance.why_it_matters: Establishes the massive radioactive payload that made the reentry so dangerous.

substance.claim: On 24 January 1978, the satellite reentered the atmosphere, scattering debris along a 600-kilometre path from Great Slave Lake to Baker Lake.
substance.why_it_matters: Defines the geographical scale of the disaster.

substance.claim: Recovered fragments displayed radioactivity of up to 1.1 sieverts per hour, a level sufficient to kill a person remaining in contact for a few hours.
substance.why_it_matters: Quantifies the immediate lethal threat posed by the scattered debris.

substance.claim: The Canadian government billed the Soviet Union Can$6,041,174.70 for cleanup costs under the 1972 Space Liability Convention.
substance.why_it_matters: Highlights the unprecedented legal and financial burden of the incident.

substance.claim: A similar RORSAT satellite failed in 1973, dropping its reactor into the Pacific Ocean north of Japan.
substance.why_it_matters: Contextualizes Kosmos 954 as part of a pattern of Soviet nuclear space failures.

description: The Soviet Union dropped a nuclear reactor from space onto Canada. Here is how Kosmos 954 turned the sky into a radiation hazard.
end_screen_followup: Every Type Of Star Explained in 10 minutes

beats.narration: Kosmos 954 carried a BES-5 reactor. Inside sat fifty kilograms of highly-enriched uranium. Over ninety percent was uranium-235. By December 1977 it had drifted off course, and the system meant to boost the spent core into a safe disposal orbit had failed. Then it fell. On 24 January 1978, the satellite reentered the atmosphere. Debris scattered along a six-hundred-kilometer path. It stretched from Great Slave Lake to Baker Lake. Searchers found fragments reading up to 1.1 sieverts per hour. One piece was hot enough to kill a person who stayed beside it for a few hours. The cleanup began in the snow. It was called Operation Morning Light.
beats.visual: Archival footage of satellite reentry, map showing debris trail across Canada, close-up of radiation gauge spiking, workers in hazmat suits in blizzard conditions.

beats.narration: The damage cost millions. Canada billed the Soviet Union. The invoice totaled Can$6,041,174.70. They cited the 1972 Space Liability Convention. In secret meetings, Soviet officials had already warned the Americans they had lost control of the satellite. The cleanup lasted months. The political fallout lingered longer. This was 1978. Chernobyl came in 1986, on a far larger scale.
beats.visual: Documentary shots of the 1972 treaty, Soviet officials signing checks, split-screen comparison of Kosmos debris field and Chernobyl exclusion zone, slow pan over frozen Canadian landscape.

beats.narration: The 1973 failure dropped its reactor into the Pacific. It sank north of Japan. That silence contrasted with the open air of 1978. Here, fragments scattered across land. Recovery teams found hot metal in the snow. The pieces they found held an estimated one percent of the fuel. Moscow eventually paid three million Canadian dollars, about half the bill. It was a financial line item for radioactive waste.
beats.visual: Split screen: dark ocean depth map vs. snowy terrain with recovery gear. Graphic overlay of the dollar amount counting up. Archival footage of Canadian officials.

beats.narration: Scale defines the horror. Chernobyl emptied a city. This event contaminated a path. The reactor did not explode. It fell. It broke. The danger was invisible. The cost was political. The precedent was set.
beats.visual: Map animating the 600km debris path across Canada. Close-up of the BES-5 reactor diagram. Text overlay: 50kg U-235. Fade to black with static.
